title: Liverpool confirm agreement to sign special midfielder
description: Liverpool have confirmed an agreement to sign an exciting midfielder. The midfield is a really tricky area for Andoni Iraola to figure out at the moment.It doesn't feel like he quite has the right pro...
fullText:
Liverpool have confirmed an agreement to sign an exciting midfielder.

The midfield is a really tricky area for Andoni Iraola to figure out at the moment.

It doesn't feel like he quite has the right profiles for his system to work. Looking at how Iraola used to play at Bournemouth, he had players capable of releasing the ball quickly.

At Liverpool, things are different.

And it's not just on the ball, where the Reds' midfielders struggle. The midfield is also porous. Gaps are too easy to exploit at the moment and it makes Liverpool's overall game ineffective.

That's why things need to change. Either Liverpool's current options start to perform or Iraola has to make some difficult decisions.

Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch both like to carry the ball, and neither are extremely strong when it comes to their reprise possession.

Playing the two of them in a double pivot just doesn't make a lot of sense.

Alexis Mac Allister is a much better players suited to the system and has also started the season in great form. In addition to that Trey Nyoni's ability on the ball also makes him an ideal fit.

However, if Liverpool want an intense ball-winner who is also capable of playing out from deep in the build-up, they will need to enter the transfer market.

Lamine Camara is high on the club's shortlist and a move for him would make a lot of sense. He absolutely could fix the Reds' midfield.

The Reds did sign a midfielder in the end.

Even though the transfer window shut two weeks ago, Liverpool quietly confirmed the arrival of Patrik Farkas as a free agent on the club's official website.

Farkas has returned to the club after leaving at U16 level to join Blackburn.

He has spent the summer training with the U21s and struck an agreement to join the Reds as revealed by Anfield Watch exclusively back in June.

Now the deal has been finalised at last, and the exciting U19 Hungary midfielder has completed his move to the Reds.

He sat on the bench for the U21s against West Ham on Monday night, and becomes the fifth Hungarian on the books at Liverpool joining his younger brother Erik, Armin Pecsi, Dominik Szoboszlai and Milos Kerkez.

title: Ausilio closing in on agreement with Tottenham after 28 years with Inter
description: Multiple outlets in Italy are reporting that former Inter director Piero Ausilio is closing in on an agreement to take over as the new sporting director at Premier League club Tottenham Hotspur after ...
fullText:
Multiple outlets in Italy are reporting that former Inter director Piero Ausilio is closing in on an agreement to take over as the new sporting director at Premier League club Tottenham Hotspur after his 28-year career with the Nerazzurri.

Ausilio officially left his position as sporting director at Inter on September 2, the day after the summer transfer window had come to an end and has since been replaced by his long-term deputy Dario Baccin.

MILAN, ITALY – MAY 17: (L-R) vice Sportif director Dario Baccin, director Piero Ausilio, President Giuseppe Marotta, coach Cristian Chivu and Vice President Javier Zanetti pose for a photo with the Coppa Campioni d'Italia and Coppa Italia trophies following the Serie A match between FC Internazionale and Hellas Verona FC at Giuseppe Meazza Stadium on May 17, 2026 in Milan, Italy. (Photo by Marco Luzzani/Getty Images)

Ausilio had originally joined Inter as a secretary with the youth teams all the way back in the late 1990s before progressing through various roles and eventually into the position of sporting director, a role that he held for well over a decade.

The Nerazzurri won three Serie A titles, three Coppa Italias and three trophies in the Supercoppa Italiana as well as reaching the Champions League final twice and the Europa League final once.

Reports over the weekend suggested that Ausilio had been approached by Tottenham to take over as sporting director following the end of his time in San Siro.

CAGLIARI, ITALY – AUGUST 28: Piero Ausilio sporting director of Inter looks on during the Serie A TIM match between Cagliari Calcio and FC Internazionale at Sardegna Arena on August 28, 2023 in Cagliari, Italy. (Photo by Enrico Locci/Getty Images)

Now, according to reports from various outlets in Italy including La Gazzetta dello Sport, Ausilio is closing in on an agreement with Tottenham. The Pink Papers claims that it is looking like a matter of 'when' and not 'if' Ausilio goes to Spurs.

He would find several Italian connections in North London, most obviously head coach Roberto De Zerbi and players Sandro Tonali and Destiny Udogie.

Ausilio would also be the second Italian sporting director at Tottenham following the tenure of Fabio Paratici, who is now at the helm at Fiorentina.

title: 'A tinge of disappointment' but Addicks are going well
description: Fan writer Paul Sullivan weighs up a disappointing game against Portsmouth with a solid start to Charlton Athletics' season.
fullText:
Two consecutive home 0-0 draws against Queens Park Rangers and Portsmouth have kept Charlton ticking over in the Championship.

I was very happy to take a battling point against QPR, who are recognised as a dangerous outfit and indeed dominated possession for long periods.

There was a tinge of disappointment at not defeating 17th-placed Pompey in a fledgling Championship table.

Charlton showed good fluidity in the first half and should have been rewarded, with Millenic Alli glaringly missing in front of the Portsmouth fans who were cheering him on last season but jeering this time.

Portsmouth emerged after the interval having absorbed and escaped Charlton's pressure, putting together quicker combinations and attacking the spaces more effectively. Their best chance fell to Abu Kamara, but Arthur Okonkwo went down well to his left to thwart him. Charlton regained control in the latter stages.

Very much like last season, we generally look sound defensively, but where are the goals coming from?

Three blanks on the spin, but you can also put a positive spin on that: just one defeat in our opening seven league games.

I'm sure all Charlton fans would have taken that when we were under starters' orders on August 15, and it has resulted in a sixth-place berth.

Away from the action, Nathan Jones has once again underlined his credentials as a stand-up comedian should he ever want to jack in the football job.

Jones himself provided the punchlines, joking that when he queried the disallowed goal v QPR, the assistant referee looked at him as if he had just volleyed his cat.

He also quipped after the Portsmouth game, that one of last season's shots seemed to have come from as far away as Blackheath, a couple of miles from Charlton - a memorable dig at Thomas Kaminski's goalkeeping.

Long may Jones remain our manager, and hopefully he is never tempted to return to God's Own Country if Mr Tan ever loses patience with Brian Barry-Murphy at Cardiff City, who are our next opponents.

There were one or two raised eyebrows when Jones was pipped to August's manager of the month award by Swansea City head coach Vitor Matos, following our maximum league haul. The Swans accrued two fewer points than Charlton.

Even perfection is not rewarded now.

So we journey from one Valley to several valleys on Saturday, hoping to avoid Cardiff taking their frustrations out on us by finally turning their plethora of missed chances into goals - and recording their first win of the season.

title: McBurnie & seven uncapped names in Scotland squad
description: Hull City forward Oli McBurnie is called up to the Scotland squad for the first time in five years while seven uncapped make new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli's first selection.
fullText:
Hull City forward Oli McBurnie has been called up to the Scotland squad for the first time in five years while uncapped Luis Binks, Colby Donovan, Jon McCracken, Josh McPake and Stephen Welsh also makes new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli's first selection.

As expected, Stoke City defender Luke Graham and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure receive their first senior call-ups.

Scott Bain, Josh Doig, Lennon Miller and James Wilson are all recalled.

McBurnie, 30, first featured for his country in 2018 and won the last of his 16 caps in 2021. He has never scored for Scotland but did net one of the penalties in the shootout that sealed a place at the delayed Euro 2020 finals.

Brondby's Binks, 25, has previously played age grade football for England and Scotland while fellow defender Donovan, 20, has come to prominence filling in for injured Canada right-back Alistair Johnston in Celtic's side this season. Like McBurnie, he has been capped at under-19 and under-21 level.

Graham was part of Scotland's pre-World Cup training camp in May after a breakthrough campaign with Dundee, winning the Scottish Premiership club's players' player and young player of the year awards.

The 22-year-old was an unused substitute in the country's send-off friendly win against Curacao, which was also Steve Clarke's last game in the dugout at Hampden Park.

The defender, who has three caps at under-21 level, has started strongly for The Potters in the Championship, who are unbeaten in their last four games, with Graham an ever-present.

Four-times capped Falkirk goalkeeper Bain and Bradford City keeper Jon McCracken were in squads named by Pocognoli's predecessor Steve Clarke.

Winger McPake and attacking club-mate James Wilson are recognised for their early-season performances at Hearts while Swansea City defender Stephen Welsh may also win his first cap.

Former Rangers academy product Ure was in demand across Europe after a free-scoring spell - 20 goals and three assists in 20 matches - that took Sirius to the top of the table in Sweden and it resulted in a £5.5m summer transfer to La Liga with Sevilla.

Time for Pocognoli to pick - who could be named in new-look Scotland squad?

Stoke best place for me to take step up - Graham

Is Sevilla's 'all-round striker' Ure ready to lead Scotland's attack?

Ure, also 22, has yet to find the target in Spain, but given his eligibility for Ukraine, the new head coach appears tempted to tie him down as soon as possible.

Since Poconogli was announced as Clarke's successor - the former Kilmarnock manager having resigned after the Scots failed to qualify for the knockout stages of a major tournament for the first time - the expectation was that the Belgian would look to freshen up an ageing squad.

His countryman, Heart of Midlothian head coach Wouter Vrancken, was "confident" there would be a few players from the Tynecastle club included.

His front three of striker James Wilson and wingers Calvin Miller and Josh McPake have been receiving plaudits for their recent performances but Miller misses out.

Former Scotland captain Scott Brown too had high hopes for the Hearts wingers, who have heavily contributed to their side's strong start to the season.

Pocognoli will take charge of Scotland for the first time on Saturday, 26 September in the Scots' Nations League B opener against Slovenia and his debut in the Hampden dugout will be three days later against Switzerland.

title: Roberto De Zerbi confirms Richarlison decision ahead of Liverpool clash
description: Tottenham Leave Richarlison Out Again Ahead of Liverpool Carabao Cup ClashTottenham travel to Anfield short on goals and without Richarlison, after Roberto De Zerbi confirmed the striker will again be...
fullText:
Tottenham travel to Anfield short on goals and without Richarlison, after Roberto De Zerbi confirmed the striker will again be left out for the Carabao Cup tie against Liverpool.

There is no ambiguity here. The player wants out, the club tried to move him on, nothing got done, and now he remains stuck between contracts, squads and plans. For Spurs, it is a poor place to be, particularly after back to back 0-0 draws against Nottingham Forest and Everton exposed a familiar problem in front of goal.

De Zerbi made it plain that the cup tie changes nothing. "Richarlison, you already know everything, nothing has changed for the Carabao Cup or Premier League. The situation is the same (he will not be involved)," De Zerbi said on Monday.

That tells you all you need to know. Richarlison was left out of Tottenham's Premier League squad earlier this month, and despite being eligible for the Carabao Cup, he still will not feature. This is a football decision shaped by a broken relationship.

Richarlison pushed to leave during the summer window and also rejected a contract extension. De Zerbi wanted to keep last season's top scorer, but there was never any appetite to force the issue if the player had already made up his mind.

Spurs then explored exits late in the window. Everton were part of that conversation, but a return stalled over personal terms. Similar problems emerged in talks with Trabzonspor and Vasco Da Gama. In short, interest existed, agreement did not.

The result is the worst outcome for everyone. Tottenham do not have the player available, Richarlison does not have the move he wanted, and the squad carries an avoidable distraction into a difficult game at Anfield.

De Zerbi did not try to dress it up. "I said last press conference, I know what happened in the last 45 days. It's not right if I explain. It's not my behaviour." He added, "It is the relationship and the problem is with the player and the club. I spoke with him many times to convince him to stay and he didn't want to. I can't go [about] every day to pray for him to stay."

That is blunt, and fair enough. Tottenham now need goals, with or without Richarlison. Liverpool away is no place for sentiment.

title: DeSean Jackson displeased with DSU's play as tough test at USF looms
description: Hornets weren't as polished as coach hoped in too-close win over Division II foe
fullText:
Coach DeSean Jackson felt his Delaware State football team may have overlooked last week's foe Division II Bowie State.

The Hornets still prevailed 21-6, though they weren't as dominant or proficient as Jackson had hoped.

DSU outgained Bowie State 391-287 in total yards and punted three times – once more than the visitors – but had drives stopped by an interception and two missed field goals. Bowie State possessed the football for 7½ minutes more than DSU while converting 7 of 14 third downs to the Hornets' 2 of 8.

"First and foremost, I'm happy about the win," Jackson said Sept. 14. "I'm just not impressed with the way we went out there and played.

"I just felt like there were a lot of things during that game that we kind of just shot ourselves in the foot."

Such self-inflicted wounds will be even costlier this week for the Hornets.

They'll visit FBS-level South Florida on Sept. 19 at 7 p.m. at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa. That's familiar ground for Jackson, who played two years there with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2017 and 2018 and made periodic visits with other NFL teams.

A LIFE TOO SHORT: DSU player's death from CTE inspires foundation to aid, educate

USF, a member of the American Conference, is 2-0 with wins over Florida International 19-9 and Army 28-24.

Delaware State improved to 2-1 with the win over Bowie State. That followed a win over Stony Brook and loss to William & Mary in which the Hornets had six turnovers but outgained the Tribe and had a fourth-quarter comeback thwarted.

Jackson hasn't yet seen this year's team develop the mindset or exhibit the execution that fueled last year's success in an 8-4 season.

"We're not in a position where we're good enough just to walk on the field and just think our talent is going to win football games," he said. "I told my team this is a very different team than we had last year.

"Year in and year out, you're gonna lose guys. Guys will graduate and you understand that. But the brand of football is gonna always remain the same."

That hasn't happened, however. The quarterback situation has also remained unresolved.

Troy transfer Ui Ale started the first two games but was relieved by William & Mary transfer Noah Brannock against the Tribe. He engineered DSU's rally in that game and started against Bowie State, but was then replaced by Ale in the second quarter.

Coastal Carolina transfer Samari Collier also saw QB duty against Stony Brook but has since been limited by a shoulder injury.

"We're just still trying to figure it out," Jackson said. "Consistency is a big thing and we just don't feel like we're as consistent as we need to be. No one's really took over that position . . . Those two [Ale and Brannock] right now are in a huge battle."

title: London loses out to Nairobi in bid to host 2029 World Athletics Championships
description: Nairobi, Kenya will be the first African host of athletics’ biggest event outside the Olympic Games
fullText:
London has lost out on hosting rights for the 2029 World Athletics Championships, with the event instead to be held in Africa for the first time.

Nairobi, Kenya submitted the winning bid, beating other candidate cities Rome, London and Munich for the rights to host athletics' biggest event outside the Olympic Games.

The hosts for the next two editions were announced in a World Athletics conference in Budapest, which has just hosted the inaugural Ultimate Championships, on Tuesday.

World Athletics president Seb Coe said "the interest in hosting our world championships has frankly never been higher" and praised "the quality, commitment and ambition demonstrated by all four... outstanding bids".

He said: "Taking our championships to Africa for the first time will be historic. Nairobi has presented a compelling and an emotional bid.

"This is a fast-growing, dynamic, modern metropolis that serves as the economic, cultural, and political hub of East Africa.

"Kenya is one of the great athletics nations. The sport is woven into the fabric of the country, and athletes such as world gold medallists Faith Kipyegon, Vivian Cheruiyot, Eliud Kipchoge, Hellen Obiri and David Rudisha, as well as two-time Olympic champion Kip Keino, multiple world cross-country champion Paul Tergat and multiple world half marathon champion Tegla Loroupe, have shaped the history of our sport.

"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances. Nairobi has demonstrated emphatically that this is their moment to supercharge our sport, leaving a compelling legacy that inspires a continent."

Nairobi had submitted a bid for the 2025 edition but lost out to Tokyo, where it finished second in the medal table.

Munich was awarded host status for the 2031 edition of the biennial championships, which takes place in September at the end of the athletics season. It will be the third time Germany has hosted the event but first in the Bavarian capital.

Coe said: "Germany has proved time and again that it is an outstanding and dependable host for major athletics events. Berlin 2009 remains one of the memorable editions of the World Championships, and we have since seen tremendous support for the sport at the European Championships in Berlin and Munich."

However, the decision is a major blow to London, which had been seen as a frontrunner in the race. The UK government threw its weight behind the 2029 bid, with London Stadium - the arena purpose-built for the 2012 Olympics - intended to be the host venue.

But there were challenges even getting it off the ground in the form of needing to smooth relations with Championship football club West Ham, which had earlier argued it had priority to the stadium during the football season.

A deal was reached involving the London mayor's office, Athletic Ventures - a joint venture of UK bodies responsible for organising major events including the London Diamond League - and the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, which satisfied West Ham and meant the bid could go ahead. It was finally submitted last month.

But the public back-and-forth with the club was unlikely to inspire confidence in the World Athletics Council, while sparse crowds at the European Championships in Birmingham's Alexander Stadium this summer - despite being in a different city and in different circumstances - may also have damaged its standing.

Asked whether the West Ham saga played a role in London's failure, Coe refused to comment, saying: "I'm not going to maintain a running commentary today on the judgement and the basis of those judgements."

Jack Buckner, chief executive of UK Athletics and co-founder of Athletic Ventures, said: "We are deeply disappointed that the 2029 World Athletics Championships will not be held in London. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels.

"The UK is an incredible host for major sports events and the British public loves athletics. Athletic Ventures has the ambition to bring those events here and, although today's announcement hasn't gone our way, we will review and regroup. We know the world's athletes love competing here and we'll continue to explore further opportunities to make that happen.

"Our congratulations go to Nairobi and we wish the organising committee all the best for a great event in 2029."

London Stadium has not hosted an athletics championships since a highly successful 2017 edition, when Mo Farah won 10,000m gold and 5,000m silver and Britain took a surprise victory in the men's 4x100m relay. That event broke an eight-year record for ticket sales at a world championships, with more than 660,000 sold.

While the stadium has not hosted another major championships since 2017 it has welcomed the annual London Diamond League. A sellout crowd of 60,000 watched Scot Josh Kerr break the mile world record at this July's meet.

However that success was not enough to persuade World Athletics to choose the capital from the four candidates. London had specifically bid for the 2029 edition, while both Nairobi and Munich had indicated their willingness to host either in 2029 and 2031.

Beijing will host the next edition of the world championships, in 2027.

title: Squad tweaks show Morrison's 'trust'
description: Fan writer Jonny Drury dissects why West Bromwich Albion boss James Morrison embodies the concept of football being a 'squad game'.
fullText:
How many times do we hear the phrase from managers, "it's a squad game"?

They are right, it is, but managers very rarely apply that logic. They like to keep the same side for as long as they possibly can, depending on injuries.

We have seen it at Albion, certainly under Carlos Corberan when he had a slender squad, would hardly change things, and injuries would bite.

Flip that on its head and in the first handful of games of this season James Morrison has made a change in almost every single game.

In some outings there have been multiple, and some haven't always gone down well with the supporters.

Take the exclusion of Jimmy-Jay Morgan from the starting line-up against QPR for example. No one saw that coming.

Other key players have stepped out and then back in.

Some would argue that tinkering like that upsets the rhythm of the side, but it hasn't at all.

In fact, what it has outlined is that Morrison has something that a lot of other managers, who claim football is a 'squad game', don't have.

That is trust in all the players he has at his disposal. And that is a real positive as Albion try and kick on from a superb start to the campaign.

Players have come in and done a job, which in turn has seen Morrison develop trust in them.

There will be ups and downs, it won't always be this good. But for the first time in a while, Albion seem to have a capable squad who are all backed by the manager, and that can only be a good thing.

title: Cardiff to host 2029 women's Champions League final
description: Uefa have confirmed a number of host appointments for upcoming finals, with Cardiff's Principality Stadium set to host the 2029 women's Champions League final.
fullText:
Cardiff's Principality Stadium will host the women's Champions League final in 2029.

The 73,931-seater venue hosted the men's final between Real Madrid and Juventus in 2017 and will now welcome Europe's elite female talents later this decade.

"It's brilliant news for Cymru and the FAW and the journey that we're on, particularly in the women's game," said Football Association of Wales (FAW) chief executive Noel Mooney.

It comes nine years after Cardiff City Stadium hosted the women's Champions League final between Paris Saint-Germain and Lyon - with the latter winning on penalties following a goalless draw after extra-time.

The Cardiff city centre venue will be named National Stadium of Wales for the event to comply with Uefa sponsorship rules.

Mooney added: "This is about much more than one night in 2029. Our ambition is for the Uefa women's Champions League final to become a catalyst for the continued transformation of women's and girls' football in Wales."

Earlier this year, Principality Stadium - the largest stadium in Wales - hosted the FA Community Shield as reigning Premier League champions Arsenal won 3-0 against Manchester City.

"This is a hugely significant moment for women's sport in Wales and across Europe," said Welsh Rugby Union group chief executive Abi Tierney.

"We are absolutely delighted that our stadium has been selected to host the 2029 Uefa women's Champions League final, bringing one of the biggest occasions in world football to Cardiff and Wales.

"The rapid growth of women's sport continues to inspire new generations of athletes and supporters, and hosting an event of this magnitude at the National Stadium of Wales is a powerful statement about the importance and future of the women's game."

Uefa have also confirmed Munich will host the 2028 men's Champions League final with Barcelona staging the final a year later, 30 years on from Manchester United's dramatic triumph over Bayern Munich in the Spanish city.

The 2028 women's Champions League final will take place at Parc Olympic Lyonnais.

It has also been announced that the National Arena in Bucharest will host the 2028 Europa League final. The National Stadium in Belgrade will hold the Europa League final a year later.

Turin's iconic Juventus Stadium will host the 2028 Conference League final. The Puskss Arena in Budapest will host the 2029 showpiece.

title: V/H/S SCP: When fandom meets law and Creative Commons
description: There’s a fascinating legal conflict brewing online that has really caught my attention. This story has everything: niche online communities, obscure horror fandom, internet drama, independen…
fullText:
There’s a fascinating legal conflict brewing online that has really caught my attention. This story has everything: niche online communities, obscure horror fandom, internet drama, independent film-making, misappropriation of internet culture, and Creative Commons licences. It involves SCP (Secure. Contain. Protect), a popular wiki that tells the fictional story of a foundation dedicated to “containing anomalous objects, entities, and phenomena.” The other player is A24 Films, the independent US entertainment company responsible for various cult and critical classics such as ‘The Witch’, ‘Ex Machina’, ‘Everything Everywhere All At Once’, and ‘Backrooms’.

One thing before we begin, I was completely unfamiliar with SCP before I started looking into this (thanks to KeyTryer for bringing this to my attention), so if I get anything wrong about the community or how it is organised, feel free to correct me. It is not my intention to delve into SCP itself in too much detail, and I am aware that every online community has its own lore, so I’m open to corrections and clarifications.

SCP is a collaborative Wiki that documents a fictional foundation that protects humanity from paranormal phenomena. The stated purpose of this organisation is:

“We operate to maintain normalcy, so that the worldwide civilian population can live and go on with their daily lives without fear, mistrust, or doubt in their personal beliefs, and to maintain human independence from extraterrestrial, extradimensional, and other extranormal influence.”

The history of the project itself is the stuff of Internet legend, and it is a great example of the collaborative power of the Web. This is not a planned universe, but it is mostly driven by anonymous contributions. It originated in 2007 with a post on 4chan’s paranormal board in the format of official government documents describing a statue that required “special containment procedures.” The style makes me think of the ‘X-Files’, ‘Cabin in the Woods’, ‘Hellboy’, and even a bit of Indiana Jones, with a hint of a conspiratorial-yet-mundane writing style. Horror disguised in a matter-of-fact style. This format proved very popular, and other users imitated it, added new objects, and these gradually coalesced into a secret organisation responsible for containing them. These origins have now been incorporated into the existing site in the shape of archived posts.

The first dedicated SCP wiki was created in January 2008, and this is where the community began standardising the familiar features of SCP writing. This includes numbered files, standard official-sounding prose, containment procedures, object classes such as Safe, Euclid and Keter, and recurring concepts including D-class personnel and Site-19. I think that the site’s popularity is precisely in this shared language and formatting, which makes shared participation and collaboration easier to achieve. The current site has typical wiki functionalities such as forums and page discussions, also enhancing the collaborative nature of the project.

During the following years, SCP evolved from a collection of short entries into a vast collaborative fictional project. During this time, writers added longer SCP files. The site moved to other formats, with comic adaptations, as well as conventional stories called “Tales”. The universe grew with various other organisations and overlapping canons, making it a rich fictional universe where various stories can co-exist. The idea here is one of a permanent fog of war: the narrators are always unreliable, and the records may be inaccurate or incomplete. The absence of a true canon make collaboration and further stories more viable. Articles are individually authored, discussed and rated; poorly received pages may be deleted.

The popularity of the site has led to it being replicated in several languages, as well as being used in other media such as games, videos, podcasts, novels, and artwork. The project is perhaps one of the most successful examples of the use of Creative Commons in collaborative fiction and entertainment, as the Wiki is published under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike Unported 3.0 licence (more on that later).

The remarkable thing about SCP is that there is no real-life legal foundation, the Foundation itself is the fictional entity. Therefore, the SCP universe has not been created or controlled by a conventional publisher or central author. SCP grew from anonymous folklore, creepypasta, obscure forums, and has morphed into something close to an open-source literary universe. SCP is governed by an amorphous collective, but is made up of individually authored contributions.

I’m a bit surprised that I didn’t know about this project, it ticks many boxes for me, but in my defence I have never been into horror. Browsing the site, I realise that I was peripherally aware of a lot of the art and themes, as well as some of the depicted threats, just things I often encounter online (such as the non-existent antimemetics division). But this is a remarkable story of the power of the Commons in storytelling. What could possibly go wrong?

Fast forward to 2026, and conflict is in the air, and it involves yet another little-known horror franchise. There is a horror series that started in 2012 called V/H/S, sort of Blair-Witch Project-style ‘found’ amateur video (apologies for the comparison, I’m not a horror buff). The original film is a series of tapes with separate stories, and there have been several additions to the franchise. A24 Films recently purchased the distribution rights to the V/H/S franchise, and also announced a new addition to the series, and it is called ‘V/H/S: SCP’, which brings together two exceptionally niche and yet wildly popular online phenomena. The idea appears to be that the new film will feature short unconnected stories in the V/H/S format, but set in the SCP universe.

Great commercial idea, right? Well, sort of.

Apparently, A24 did not licence the SCP property at all, nobody contacted them, and the project seems to rely entirely on the CC licences. And A24 has form here, their commercial success ‘Backrooms‘ is based on a sort of similar piece of online horror lore, the Backrooms universe, which also started life in the 4chan /x/ board as a form of creepypasta describing an endless maze of damp carpet, fluorescent lights, and monotonous yellow rooms. There’s also a Wiki describing the various levels and monsters, and even a series of YouTube found-footage films. I could write an entire blog post about Backrooms, but that will have to wait.

It is easy to see how A24 would be willing to look for similar stories given the enormous success of ‘Backrooms’, and SCP seems like the perfect source material: a popular horror universe with hundreds of potential stories to mine and nebulous legal status. What’s not to like?

The SCP Foundation (the real entity, not the fictional one) has now issued a statement in which they say:

“The staff and authors of the SCP Foundation Wiki (the real-life writing project behind the SCP Foundation universe and its official home) were not consulted or contacted regarding this film. We have been attempting to contact the filmmakers but haven’t yet been successful. To be clear: we have not had any communication with the filmmakers, producers, or distributors for this project, despite our best efforts, and to the best of our knowledge they have not made any efforts to contact us. Furthermore, A24 does not and cannot have any exclusive rights to anything related to the SCP Foundation, including any films that Spooky Pictures or anyone else may choose to create. […]

We’d love to sit down with A24, Spooky Pictures, and other involved parties to discuss options for how they could make and distribute a film while complying with CC BY-SA. We chose to release our project under a Creative Commons license to allow fans to tell their own stories as well as adapt ours. We chose the ShareAlike license to ensure that everyone who enjoyed those fan works would have the same rights as the people who created them. We hope that the filmmakers will follow their legal obligations under our license.”

There’s no legal threat here (yet), but an invitation for A24 to play nice with the community and open a conversation. A24 has the rights for V/H/S, but not SCP, so they made a statement to Kotaku:

“A spokesperson for A24 told Kotaku that the company is “not asserting any right to prevent others from creating their own SCP-based works” and that V/H/S: SCP is intended to be a “tribute” to the greater SCP universe.

“A24’s ‘worldwide rights’ cover the next film in the V/H/S franchise,” reads A24’s statement. “It is not a claim of exclusivity over the SCP Foundation universe or its concepts, and we’re not asserting any right to prevent others from creating their own SCP-based works… The project is in development and is meant as a tribute to the community that created this world.””

A tribute? Really? So what is going on? Could SCP eventually sue A24 for copyright infringement?

This is a fascinating question, and for one, I’m delighted as I now have a huge amount of material for my Film class and my Creative Commons class.

The first thing to consider is the nature of the authorship of SCP and all of its related materials. It may be easy to think of collaborative online projects such as SCP and Backrooms as some sort of res nullius, something that has no owner, pretty much content that is in the public domain, but nothing could be further from the truth. Like anything else, collaborative media such as wikis do have copyright, wiki contributors generally retain copyright in their original contributions, stories, and artwork. They license those contributions both to the public and to the platform; they do not normally assign ownership to the website. Many of the SCP stories and articles have an author, many writing anonymously, and even in the situation in which a contribution has several authors, these would be considered joint authors. Editors who have exercised sufficient creative editorial control could also claim ownership if the arrangement is sufficiently original. As mentioned above, over the years there have been related media such as comics and games, and those have their own copyright and authors. Furthermore, SCP doesn’t have a brand or a registered trademark; a few years ago a Russian national tried to register the SCP mark, but after some crowdfunding and online outrage, the registration was removed.

There are some issues about anonymous works that I won’t cover here, as jurisdictions deal with this in different ways, but just for completeness, anonymous works do have copyright even when the author cannot be identified, although anonymity may complicate ownership and practical enforcement.

So SCP authors have copyright, but as mentioned earlier, the wiki is released under a CC-BY-SA 3.0 licence. As someone who helped in the drafting process of the 4.0 CC licence, it still pains me to see that projects never updated to the 4.0 licence, but I digress… This licence is generally quite broad, it allows for commercial uses of the work, for example, but it has two very important conditions. The first is attribution, other people may adapt and commercialise SCP material provided that they give attribution to the author; as most SCP articles have authors, this usually takes the form of “X is based on SCP-X by ‘AuthorY'”. The trickiest restriction is the ShareAlike condition, this is a typical copyleft clause which means that any derivative material must be released under the same licence. This is something similar to the licence I use in this blog, except that mine does not allow for commercial uses.

So, in order to be able to use the SCP stories in its upcoming film, A24 has to comply with these requirements, as well as some other conditions, such as the fact that no derivative can use technological protection measures or digital rights management (DRM). This would mean that the film itself has to be released under CC-BY-SA (I would argue that they can use version 4.0 of the licence), with no DRM, and they have to attribute the stories used. If they don’t, then they would be infringing copyright, and the authors could sue A24 for copyright infringement.

Whoever said that copyright was not fun?

V/H/S: SCP is set to be released in 2027, so it is still too early to say if they will comply with the terms of the licence. A24 has already found itself in hot water when it issued some automated takedowns of Backrooms artwork, something for which they apologised. I’m sure that A24 employs expensive lawyers, and that they will have gone through all of this internally, so I would not be surprised if we see the film released under a CC licence with adequate community attribution. Edit: another option would be not use any SCP stories, just the unprotected SCP brand.

However, A24 is operating in a new space, using Internet culture and memes as the new source of commercial success, so it makes no sense that they would willingly antagonise the very communities that have given rise to these properties.

In the end, this opens a wider conversation about the trend of independent film companies trying to tap into the wealth of creativity that can be found online. In a world that is increasingly tired of endless sequels and superhero slop, savvy studios are turning to online creators. Audiences are thirsty for original stories, and many of those can be found in surprising corners of the Web.

But these studios should also respect the collaborative and permissive nature of these communities, including the very re-use and remix culture that allows such creativity to flourish.

As Pulp said: ‘Cause everybody hates a tourist, especially one who, who thinks it’s all such a laugh.’

title: Measuring Gauss-Seidel loop-carried dependency and fixing it via loop unrolling
description: The art of unrolling.
fullText:
Last time, we explored the Gauss-Seidel method. We arrived at the following conclusion: the math says Gauss-Seidel takes half as many iterations to converge, and this is backed up by our numerical test case. Yet, despite requiring only half the number of iterations, the Gauss-Seidel solver takes 4 to 5 times as long as the Jacobi one. A seemingly puzzling fact if you think about it: how can a method which is better on paper perform worse when implemented numerically? As we’ve seen, the explanation lies in that, unlike Jacobi, the Gauss-Seidel update rule has loop-carried dependencies which prevent the compiler from vectorizing the code. The question we’ll try to answer today thus is: is this the end of the road or can we somehow recover Gauss-Seidel’s convergence advantage without sacrificing the hardware efficiency of Jacobi?

And it turns out that, yes you can! We have two different routes though: one fairly general where you help the compiler as much as you can (but you need to understand a bit how compilers and CPUs work), and another, quite specific to our particular 2D Poisson test case, where you let the math guide you. None of them will be a smooth ride, but we’ll learn a lot along the way. Eventually, we’ll explore both, but for now we’ll ride along the first one and discover what loop unrolling is.

Let’s rewind for a second. Last time, we pitted two update rules against each other on the same 2D Poisson problem: the humble Jacobi iteration, and its slightly more sophisticated cousin, Gauss-Seidel.

Jacobi always reads from the old iterate v and writes into a fresh array u. Gauss-Seidel, in contrast, updates in place:

That is a one-line difference that buys you a faster-converging method, at exactly half the number of sweeps to reach a given tolerance. On paper, Gauss-Seidel should win outright. And yet, when we actually ran the numbers, Gauss-Seidel took 4 to 5 times longer than Jacobi, wall-clock, despite needing only half as many iterations. Something in that one-line difference is costing us dearly, and it isn’t showing up anywhere in the convergence theory.

Loop-carried dependencies, made concrete

The culprit, as we found, is that u(i-1,j) in the Gauss-Seidel update has already been overwritten by the time you read it. It’s not the old value from the previous sweep, it’s this sweep’s freshly computed neighbor. That’s precisely what makes Gauss-Seidel converge faster: you’re propagating information within a single sweep instead of waiting a full iteration for it. But it also means iteration i cannot start until iteration i-1 has fully finished writing u(i-1,j). Jacobi has no such constraint: every read in a Jacobi sweep comes from v, which nothing in that sweep ever touches.

This is the textbook definition of a loop-carried dependency, and it’s exactly the kind of thing a compiler needs to reason about before deciding whether it can vectorize a loop, reorder instructions, or overlap iterations on an out-of-order core. Jacobi: no such dependency, compiler’s hands are free. Gauss-Seidel: hard dependency, compiler’s hands are tied.

That’s a nice story, but it’s still just a story until you can measure it. So this time, rather than taking the compiler’s word for it, we reached for OSACA — the Open Source Architecture Code Analyzer — and pointed it directly at the compiled assembly of both kernels.

OSACA reads a marked assembly loop and, assuming an idealized out-of-order core, reports two numbers per loop body: the critical path (CP), the length of the longest dependency chain running through one iteration in isolation, and the loop-carried dependency (LCD), the part of that chain that must cross from one iteration to the next. LCD is the number that matters here. It’s a hard floor on cycles-per-iteration, no amount of clever scheduling can get under it.

Here’s what came back for our -O3 -march=native kernels, compiled with plain do loops (no do concurrent, nothing fancy):

Two things jump out immediately. First, the critical path is identical for both kernels — 24 cycles. That makes sense: it’s essentially the same chain of floating-point operations in both cases:

along with a a load and a store. The arithmetic hasn’t changed; only what’s allowed to overlap has.

Second, and this is the whole ballgame: Jacobi’s loop-carried dependency is a throwaway 1 cycle (just the loop counter incrementing, nothing to do with the actual computation). Gauss-Seidel’s is 12 cycles, and OSACA even tells you exactly where it comes from:

Trace it back and it’s the west-neighbor term: %xmm1 holds this sweep’s freshly written u(i,j), and it gets read straight back in as u(i-1,j) on the very next loop trip. Three chained instructions — the west-neighbor add, the north-neighbor add, and the final multiply — each with 4-cycle latency, sum to exactly 12. That’s not a compiler being lazy; it’s the compiler correctly reporting that there is no way to start computing u(i,j) before u(i-1,j) exists, because the algorithm itself demands it.

The other giveaway, readable straight off the assembly without even needing OSACA, is the instruction mnemonics themselves. Jacobi’s inner loop is built entirely out of packed double-precision instructions — vaddpd, vmulpd, vfmadd213pd — each one crunching four grid points at a time in a single 256-bit AVX register. Gauss-Seidel’s inner loop uses the scalar forms of the exact same instructions — vaddsd, vmulsd, vfmadd213sd — one grid point at a time. The pd/sd suffix alone tells you, at a glance, which loop the compiler was able to vectorize and which one it wasn’t.

For each kernel, the CPU’s actual sustained cost per iteration is bounded below by both constraints at once, the throughput floor and the LCD, so the one that actually governs is whichever of the two is larger. For Gauss-Seidel, that’s the LCD (12 cycles, versus a 2.5-cycle throughput floor). For Jacobi, it’s the throughput floor (3 cycles, versus a negligible 1-cycle LCD). In other words, Gauss-Seidel is latency-bound and Jacobi is throughput-bound. Two different bottlenecks entirely, which is precisely why comparing them isn’t just a matter of reading off the same column for both.

Normalizing each kernel’s governing bound per grid point (dividing Jacobi’s by 4, since it processes four elements per vector iteration) gives a predicted per-sweep slowdown of roughly

\[\dfrac{12}{3 / 4} = 16\times\]

That’s higher than the 4–5× we measured wall-clock. But remember, wall-clock measures total time to solution, and Gauss-Seidel needs only half as many sweeps as Jacobi to converge. Once you back that out, the actual per-sweep slowdown implied by the measurements is

\[\left(\frac{T_{GS}}{T_J}\right) \Big/ \left(\frac{N_{GS}}{N_J}\right) \approx (4\text{–}5) \times 2 \approx 8\text{–}10\times\]

which lands within a factor of two of OSACA’s prediction, a healthy level of agreement for a static model that has zero visibility into the memory system. The mechanism OSACA identifies — Gauss-Seidel latency-bound at a hard 12-cycle wall, Jacobi comfortably throughput-bound — is exactly right, even if the precise number needs a pinch of salt.

So, the diagnosis is confirmed in triplicate: theory, static analysis, and measurement all agree. Gauss-Seidel’s faster convergence is bought entirely at the price of a serialized, 12-cycle-per-element dependency chain that the compiler simply cannot break on its own. Which raises the obvious question: is that dependency chain fundamental to the algorithm, or is it an artifact of how we happened to write the loop?

Loop unrolling is one of the oldest tricks in the optimizing-compiler playbook, and the idea is disarmingly simple. Instead of executing a loop body once per iteration and paying the overhead of a branch and a counter update every single time, you write out the body two, four, or eight times per iteration, advancing the counter by that many steps at once.

Take a trivial example, nothing to do with our Poisson problem yet:

Unrolled by a factor of two, this becomes:

modulo a bit of bookkeeping if n is odd, which we’ll conveniently ignore for now. Fewer branches, fewer counter increments, and — crucially — twice as much independent work exposed to the compiler within a single loop trip. That last point is really the whole appeal: with two statements sitting side by side and no dependency between them, the compiler is free to interleave them, pack them into a single vector instruction, or schedule them however the hardware likes. Unrolling doesn’t make the CPU do less work; it makes the scheduler’s job easier by giving it more to look at at once. So, naturally, the question we should ask is: does the same trick save Gauss-Seidel?

A tempting shortcut that doesn’t work

Let’s try the obvious thing and unroll our Gauss-Seidel inner loop by two, changing nothing else:

Look closely at the second statement: it reads u(i,j) which is exactly the value the first statement just finished computing, two lines above. We haven’t removed the loop-carried dependency at all. We’ve just moved a copy of it inside the loop body, where it’s now a same-iteration dependency instead of a cross-iteration one. The compiler still can’t touch these two statements independently, still can’t vectorize them together, and still has to execute them strictly in order. We’ve paid for the bookkeeping of unrolling (larger code, an odd-n remainder to handle) and bought ourselves precisely nothing.

This is worth sitting with for a second, because it’s a genuinely common trap: unrolling looks like it should help with dependencies, since it’s so often reached for as a vectorization enabler, but by itself it does nothing whatsoever to break a true dependency chain. It’s very good at exposing parallelism that already exists (as in our trivial a(i) = 2*a(i) example) but is completely powerless against parallelism that has to be created. Gauss-Seidel falls squarely in the second category: the dependency isn’t a scheduling accident the compiler failed to notice, it’s baked into the mathematics of the update rule.

So if unrolling alone is a dead end, what’s missing? The answer is that the dependency itself has to be rewritten away before unrolling can do any good. That means reaching for a bit of algebra, not just a bit of loop restructuring.

To keep the algebra honest and readable, let’s forget about the full 2D grid for now, and work with the 1D Poisson equation, \(u'' = -f\), discretized on a uniform grid as

\[\frac{u_{i+1} - 2 u_i + u_{i-1}}{\Delta x^2} = -f_i.\]

Solving for \(u_i\) gives the update rule

\[u_i = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(u_{i-1} + u_{i+1} + \Delta x^2 f_i\right),\]

so, unsurprisingly, the constant playing the role of our earlier \(0.25\) is now \(c = \tfrac12\). Sweeping left to right and updating in place, Gauss-Seidel reads:

Exactly one neighbor here is a problem: u(i-1) was overwritten by the previous loop trip, while u(i+1) is still the untouched, old value (the sweep hasn’t reached it yet). That’s the whole dependency, laid completely bare with nothing else to distract from it.

Group everything that doesn’t depend on the sweep’s own progress into a single per-column quantity,

\[t_i = u_{i+1} + \Delta x^2 f_i,\]

which is fully known before the block starts (it’s old data, untouched by anything we’re computing right now). The update collapses to a clean, one-term affine recursion:

\[u_i = c\left(u_{i-1} + t_i\right), \qquad u_{i-1} \equiv \texttt{um},\]

where um is shorthand for the last already-updated value feeding into this block. This is precisely the shape that makes the dependency chain visible as just a recursion in \(u\) — nothing more, nothing less.

Solving the recursion two steps ahead

Rather than computing \(u_i\) and then \(u_{i+1}\) from it, we solve the recursion explicitly for both, purely in terms of quantities that existed before the block started:

\[u_i = c\,(\texttt{um} + t_i)\]

\[u_{i+1} = c\,(u_i + t_{i+1}) = c\Big(c\,(\texttt{um}+t_i) + t_{i+1}\Big) = c^2\,\texttt{um} + c^2\,t_i + c\,t_{i+1}\]

Look at what happened: \(u_{i+1}\) no longer references \(u_i\) at all. Both outputs are now pure functions of um, \(t_i\), and \(t_{i+1}\). All quantities that existed before this pair of updates began. The intra-pair dependency that plain unrolling couldn’t touch (the “unroll-only” kernel from the previous section) has been algebraically dissolved.

In code, defining \(c_2 \equiv c^2\), this gives the following kernel:

Two independent expressions, no read of one output by the other’s computation. Exactly what the compiler needs to schedule them concurrently instead of serially.

This is where the 1D detour pays off. In the real 2D stencil, the north, south, and source contributions play no role whatsoever in creating the i-dependency — they’re either values from a row Gauss-Seidel has already finished, or values from a row it hasn’t touched yet, but never anything the i-loop itself is computing. So they simply fold into the same lumped \(t_i\) we just defined:

\[t_i \;\longrightarrow\; \texttt{tmp}_i = \Delta x^2 b(i,j) + u(i+1,j) + u(i,j+1) + u(i,j-1),\]

and the exact same two-line substitution applies, verbatim, giving you the unrolled kernel:

The trailing if block just mops up a leftover column when n is odd, i.e. the same remainder bookkeeping any unrolled loop needs, nothing conceptually new.

Ok, so the new kernel looks a bit more complicated than our original one. But mathematically, it’s all the same thing, so is it truly more efficient? Time to check the theory against the machine. Same workflow as before: compile with -O3 -march=native -S, mark the inner loop, and let OSACA loose on it.

If you look at the last two columns, two things should stand out. The critical path CP got a bit longer, but the loop-carried dependencies (LCD) dropped from 12 to 4 cycles per loop trip — and since each trip now covers two elements, that’s roughly a 6× drop per grid point.

That’s the static prediction. Time to see if the actual machine agrees — and, more interestingly, to see why it agrees, one compilation flag at a time.

Experiment 1 — baseline, no optimization

First, a sanity check. Compiled with -O0, so no scheduling cleverness of any kind gets to play a role:

Two things worth checking here before moving on. First, all three solvers reach the solution in the same number of iterations as the earlier posts — confirming the unrolled kernel really is computing the same thing as the textbook one, algebra and all, not some subtly different (and subtly wrong) approximation. Second, at -O0, the unrolled kernel is already reliably faster than the textbook kernel, by almost exactly the ratio convergence theory predicts for Gauss-Seidel over Jacobi (2×) — a nice confirmation that even without any compiler scheduling to exploit, exposing two independent computations per loop trip buys you something, purely from halving the loop overhead. But nobody ships -O0 code, so this is a baseline, not the result.

Experiment 2 — the critical one

Now compile with real optimization, but deliberately keep vectorization switched off (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -fno-tree-vectorize), so that any gains we see can’t be attributed to SIMD at all:

This is the number that matters. With vectorization explicitly disabled, the unrolled kernel is still six times faster per sweep than the textbook kernel, and lands within 5% of Jacobi’s per-sweep cost. Since neither Gauss-Seidel kernel can be vectorized under this flag anyway, this gain has nothing to do with packing multiple grid points into one instruction. It comes entirely from something more subtle: reducing the loop-carried dependency lets the CPU’s out-of-order scheduler overlap the scalar work of consecutive iterations, filling execution ports that the textbook kernel’s 12-cycle dependency chain left idle. Fewer cycles spent waiting, same number of instructions issued. This is the empirical confirmation of the LCD-versus-throughput story from the OSACA table above, isolated from vectorization entirely.

Experiment 3 — turning vectorization back on

Finally, the same three kernels, same flags, but with vectorization allowed:

Both Gauss-Seidel kernels are completely unchanged, down to the microsecond. That’s expected once you know the assembly: gfortran never vectorizes either GS kernel regardless of this flag, so there’s nothing for the flag to act on. Vectorization was never the mechanism behind experiment 2’s speedup. It’s a separate story that only applies to Jacobi.

And even for Jacobi, notice the gain is real but modest: 166 µs → 115 µs, about 1.4×, not the ~4× you might expect from packing four doubles into a single AVX register. This is the by-product the LCD story predicted but didn’t fully explain on its own: vectorization only pays off to the extent that a kernel’s compute is the bottleneck, and Jacobi’s inner loop, despite having no loop-carried dependency at all, is largely memory-bound at this problem size. It streams through the whole grid every sweep with essentially no data reuse, so DRAM bandwidth caps the achievable speedup well below what the instruction-level analysis alone would suggest.

Put the three experiments side by side and the conclusion is unambiguous: it’s the absence (or reduction) of a loop-carried dependency, not vectorization, that lets the scheduler do its job. Vectorization is a nice bonus when it’s available. It does still help Jacobi, just less than you’d naively guess. But it was never the reason Gauss-Seidel was slow, and reducing the LCD was already enough, on its own, to close almost the entire performance gap with Jacobi. Actually, this unrolled Gauss-Seidel kernel hands us the solution almost 3 seconds faster than the Jacobi one. Mission accomplished! Or so it appears…

But look closely at the mnemonics

Here’s the detail that’s easy to miss if you only look at the CP/LCD numbers and declare victory. If you look at the far right of the OSACA output, that is the assembly for inner-most loop (i) of our kernel. Every single arithmetic instruction in that table is still a scalar op — vaddsd, vmulsd, vfmadd231sd, vfmadd132sd, all operating on individual doubles in %xmm registers, not a single packed pd instruction among them. Compare that to Jacobi’s inner loop, built entirely out of vaddpd/vmulpd/vfmadd213pd on 256-bit %ymm registers, four grid points at a time. The compiler never vectorized this loop. It didn’t need to, to hit Jacobi’s throughput. It got there by exposing two independent scalar chains (one for u(i,j), one for u(i+1,j)) that fill different execution ports at the same time, rather than by packing four elements into one instruction the way Jacobi does. The one and only place the two lanes actually meet is right at the end, at line 90: a vunpcklpd stitching the two independently-computed scalars into a single 128-bit register just before the store. That’s not vectorized computation. It’s a vectorized write of two scalar results, a small, free bonus riding on top of the real work, not the source of the speedup itself.

This distinction matters more than it might look like at first glance, and it’s the seed of the next post’s cliffhanger: because the compiler is achieving Jacobi-level throughput through instruction-level parallelism across ports rather than true SIMD, this kernel still can’t be handed a wider vector width for free, and it certainly can’t be split across threads. That tiny 4-cycle pair-to-pair dependency, however cheap, is still a sequential handoff that no do concurrent or OpenMP directive could safely break apart. We’ve matched (and even slightly exceeded) Jacobi’s single-core speed, but not its parallelizability. Those turn out to be two different prizes entirely. And only one of them is in hand.

Could we push the substitution one step further? Unroll by 4 instead of 2, and squeeze out even more performance? Not really. We’d be at risk of marginally reducing an LCD that’s already a non-issue, while greatly increasing the pressure on the CPU ports.

Here’s why. Going back to the general recursion from before,

\[u_i = c^{i+1}\,u_{-1} + \sum_{m=0}^{i} c^{i-m}\,t_m,\]

each additional element you fold into the substitution costs you one more multiply-add. By the time you reach the degree-4 unrolling, you’re resolving a 4-term cascading sum, every term weighted by its own power of \(c\). Averaged across the four outputs, that’s roughly twice the multiply-add work per element compared to degree 2. And recall where we ended up last section: the throughput floor is already the governing bound at degree 2 (2.75 cycles/element, versus an LCD of only 2.0). Doubling the arithmetic per element doesn’t touch the LCD’s role in the story at all. It just raises the throughput floor further, from the bound that’s actually constraining us. You’d be spending real port-pressure budget to shave cycles off a dependency chain that was already comfortably hidden behind other work. A losing trade, and one you can see coming from the algebra alone, without even needing to compile anything.

So degree 2 isn’t an arbitrary stopping point. It’s exactly the amount of unrolling needed to push the LCD below the throughput floor, and not a bit more. Past that point, every extra unit of unrolling is pure cost with no corresponding benefit. At least for Gauss-Seidel.

We made it: a Gauss-Seidel kernel that keeps the mathematical convergence advantage over Jacobi. Same iteration count as the textbook version, while very nearly matching Jacobi’s raw computational efficiency per sweep. A serial win on both fronts at once, which is exactly the “have your cake and eat it too” outcome we set out chasing at the start of this post.

But, there’s always a but, it’s a serial win only. The kernel is still built entirely out of scalar instructions. The compiler (gfortran 15.3) never vectorized it for my particular CPU. It got to Jacobi-level throughput through a different route (independent scalar chains sharing execution ports, not packed SIMD lanes). Worse, that tiny residual pair-to-pair dependency, however cheap, is still a genuine sequential handoff. No do concurrent, no OpenMP directive, no compiler flag can safely split this loop across threads or hand it a wider vector register, because the math still insists that pair \(k\) cannot start until pair \(k-1\) has written its result.

For a single core on a laptop, that’s a complete success. But it’s a dead end for anything that needs to scale. And scaling is, after all, the entire point of numerical computing once your grids get big enough to matter. If we want a Gauss-Seidel kernel that vectorizes and multithreads, unrolling and clever algebra won’t get us there. We’ll need to change the order in which we visit grid points altogether, which is exactly where red-black ordering comes in, next time.

Acknowledgement – I have to give credit where credit is due. It is Ivan Pribec who showed me this particular unrolling trick for Gauss-Seidel. It is also he who put osaca under my radar, so none of what I presented here would have been possible without him. Thanks a lot!

title: Suspected sabotage causes major Netherlands rail disruption
description: Trains were cancelled or delayed on Tuesday after objects were found on tracks at multiple locations.
fullText:
Parts of the Netherlands, including Amsterdam, have been hit by major rail disruption after suspected sabotage to the tracks, the country's railway infrastructure operator has said.

ProRail warned that passengers in the country's centre and north should expect cancellations and delays on Tuesday, while the closure of some level crossings could cause disruption to roads.

Pipes were attached to the tracks in multiple locations, according to local media. In a statement, ProRail said the incident appeared to be "an intentional disruption... caused by human action".

It added that no suspects or motives had been identified, but the national police unit was investigating.

The BBC has contacted police for comment.

The network's website showed that at least 15 disruptions had been recorded across the country on Tuesday, with routes to the main international airport, Schiphol, and Utrecht also affected.

Train operator Nederlandse Spoorwegen said services around Zwolle, Deventer, and Amersfoot had been disrupted.

It added that the disruption was so extensive it was "not possible" to provide a bus replacement service.

A Eurostar train from Amsterdam to Paris was also delayed due to "operational restrictions" at Amsterdam Centraal on Tuesday, although it was not clear if this was linked to wider disruption. The BBC has contacted Eurostar for further information.

ProRail said in a statement: "Materials were found at multiple locations in the track that were deliberately placed there. This causes section malfunctions. Sabotage appears to be involved".

Footage published by Dutch public broadcaster NOS on Tuesday showed police carrying what appeared to be metal pipes - about 1.5 metres (5ft) long - away from railway tracks at Veenendaal in the central Netherlands.

One train in the city of Steenwijk struck one of the objects, ProRail said, but added there were no injuries as a result.

The disruption in the Netherlands came after separate reports in French media suggested a derailment in Normandy on Friday could have been an act of sabotage.

Quick Response (QR) codes (standardized internationally under ISO/IEC 18004) are two-dimensional matrix symbologies capable of encoding alphanumeric strings, URLs, Wi-Fi credentials, and contact vCards into optical binary modules.

Unlike basic 1D barcodes that only store data horizontally in 10 to 20 digits, QR codes store data across both horizontal and vertical axes—encoding up to 7,089 numeric or 4,296 alphanumeric characters. The s0lve.it Custom QR Code Generator generates high-resolution vector and raster QR codes entirely inside your browser's private memory with zero tracking redirects, zero subscription expirations, and 100% offline privacy.

Generating dozens or hundreds of individual QR codes one-by-one is tedious and error-prone. title: A wrong turn become a nightmare
description: Ibrahim Topkaya does research at Upstate Medical University and worked as a medical doctor in his home country of Turkey.
fullText:
A medical doctor from Turkey who now works as a researcher at Upstate Medical University was detained on a trip to Niagara Falls and is now being held by immigration officials in the Batavia federal detention facility.

Ibrahim Topkaya, 33, was on a trip to Niagara Falls, N.Y., with his mother on Sept. 6. His mother was visiting from Turkey for the first time in three years.

“On the way back, there was a lot of traffic, so the GPS shifted him towards the Canadian border as a faster route,” said Omar Alsafadi, a friend of Topkaya.

After making the turn, Alsafadi said the Canadian border patrol officials gave Topkaya a document stating he did not enter the country, that he was just turning around.

“As he went to the U.S. border, he provided that paperwork and I guess that wasn’t enough for them. From there, they detained him,” Alsafadi said.

Topkaya works in the bioengineering lab to advance diabetes research, according to a recent article from Upstate Medical University. He is named as an author in numerous medical research papers.

“He was a medical doctor over in Turkey and then he’s continuing his research here in the United States,” Alsafadi said. “He’s a very well-respected researcher here,” Alsafadi said. “He spends all of his time in the research lab. I know his higher up was telling him, ‘Hey you got to get out of the lab and enjoy life.’”

Alsafadi said he even requested research materials to continue his work while in detention.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security shared the following statement with Spectrum News 1 regarding Topkaya’s detention.

“On September 6, CBP encountered Ibrahim Halil Topkaya, an illegal alien from Turkey, at the Lewiston Bridge in Lewiston, New York. CBP transferred Topkaya over to ICE custody, where he will remain pending removal proceedings and will receive due process. On June 22, 2023, Topkaya legally entered the country, but chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws. To be clear: a pending application or work authorization does NOT confer legal status in the United States,” the statement said.

However, Alsafadi said Topkaya had an approved asylum case, an active work authorization and a Social Security number, all of which he shared with Spectrum News 1.

DHS didn't immediately return a request for comment seeking clarification about his legal status when asked about his Social Security number, work authorization and approved asylum case.

The Trump administration has said it will detain and deport the “worst of the worst,” but Alsafadi said that Topkaya is not that.

“It makes you scratch your head for sure. I don’t know what the process of how they determine that stuff and I think it is definitely on the wrong side with Brahim specifically. It’s a very unfortunate situation,” Alsafadi said.

According to data from the Deportation Project, a nonprofit that requests data from the federal government about arrests, detentions and deportations, there were 1,567 arrests made in the month of July in New York, the highest number of arrests from the data available which goes back to October of 2022. The data also shows that the majority of people arrested by immigration agents do not have any criminal charges.

Alsafadi said Topkaya’s mother is distraught and extended her trip in the U.S. while they wait to see what can be done for her son.

“She hasn’t eaten. I’m trying to comfort her and make sure that she knows, everything is going to work out,” Alsafadi said. “She has just been inside talking to him as much as she can on the phone.”

While the situation is difficult, Topkaya has tried to remain positive, Alsafadi said.

“He’s trying to stay positive. He wants to keep his mind going. Like I said, he wants us to send some more of the research articles so that he can keep studying and keep up to speed with the research that’s going on,” he said.
